 A Proposed Social Security Change Could Mean Bigger Raises for Retirees
 Changing the COLA calculation formula could give retirees a bigger boost.
 By
 Paige Cerulli 
 ,
 Edited by
 Laura Hohenstein 
 Updated
 Nov. 10, 2026
 Fact checked 
 This article was subjected to a comprehensive fact-checking process. Our professional fact-checkers verify article information against primary sources, reputable publishers, and experts in the field.
 Add Us On Google
 Google Preferred Sources lets you customize your search results. By choosing to follow FinanceBuzz, you’re telling Google to prioritize content from a source you trust.
When the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) was announced on October 14, 
millions of Americans receiving Social Security senior benefits 
learned that they'd receive a benefits boost next year. Though the 
cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) helps Social Security senior benefits keep up 
with inflation, some industry experts argue the COLA should be larger, and the 
method used to calculate it should be changed. Two bills, neither of which have 
passed, seek to change that formula and provide Americans with more benefits. 
Here's what you should know about the COLA, why it might not actually be keeping 
up with inflation, and the proposed changes that might increase Social Security 
benefits.

 How the COLA is calculated
The Social Security Administration (SSA) calculates the COLA using the Consumer 
Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, the CPI-W. The SSA 
compares third-quarter CPI-W to the data from the same period in the previous 
year. If the current year's data is higher, it signifies inflation has occurred, 
and the COLA, a percentage, is applied to benefits beginning in January of the 
following year.

 The problem with the current COLA calculation
The current COLA calculation has drawn criticism from groups like Social 
Security Works, a political advocacy group. "The COLA adjustment will help. But 
it doesn't fully account for the costs that Social Security beneficiaries face," 
said Nancy Altman, President of Social Security Works, after the 2027 COLA's 
announcement. "That's because the measure used to calculate it, the CPI-W, is 
designed to reflect the costs of working people — not retirees, who spend a 
higher percentage of their income on healthcare, housing, and other bare 
necessities." 
The CPI-W tracks spending habits of workers, often who are younger and healthier 
than retirees, and it may not accurately reflect the spending of retirees. For 
example, the CPI-W may underweight certain spending categories, like healthcare, 
in which seniors spend more money. Additionally, healthcare expenses tend to 
increase faster than standard inflation, meaning the CPI-W may not fully keep up 
with seniors' spending. 
 The Boosting Benefits and COLAs for Seniors Act
Democratic Representative Nikki Budzinski introduced the Boosting Benefits and 
COLAs for Seniors Act in October 2025 in an attempt to ensure that benefits 
better reflect seniors' needs. The bill proposes that the SSA should use either 
the CPI-W or the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, the CPI-E, 
whichever is higher. 
The CPI-E reflects the spending habits of Americans aged 62 and older. It's an 
experimental price index and, though it may often outpace the CPI-W, there are 
years when the CPI-E might be lower than the CPI-W. Since the bill would require 
the use of whichever price index is higher in a given year, it might help 
maximize benefits.

 The Social Security Expansion Act
Independent Senator Bernie Sanders has also introduced the Social Security 
Expansion Act in February 2025. The bill seeks to replace the existing CPI-W 
price index with the CPI-E price index. 
Sanders' proposal to change the COLA calculation is just one part of a package 
that also proposes Social Security benefit increases and implementing Social 
Security payroll taxes on earnings above $250,000 to help generate additional 
revenue for the program. 
 The potential benefits increase using the CPI-E
According to The Senior Citizens League's October 2025 analysis, an average 
individual who retired in 1999 might have received almost $5,000 more during a 
25-year retirement if their Social Security benefits had been calculated using 
the CPI-E than the CPI-W. 
The analysis also projected that an individual retiring in 2024 might receive 
over $12,000 in additional benefits across a 25-year retirement with the CPI-E 
if long-term inflation patterns continue. 
The analysis found that the CPI-E generated a smaller benefits increase in 2019, 
2022, and 2023 than the CPI-W, but overall, the CPI-E usually resulted in a 
larger benefits increase. 
 The potential downsides to using the CPI-E
Switching to the CPI-E has its potential drawbacks. According to the Bureau of 
Labor Statistics, the CPI-E is created on a small sample, so it might not fully 
represent retirees and their spending habits. 
Using the CPI-E may also increase Social Security costs. The SSA estimates that 
using the CPI-E beginning in December 2028 might increase the annual COLA by 
about 0.15 percentage points, but it might also worsen the 75-year actuarial 
balance by 0.33% of taxable payroll. That financial hit could come as Congress 
is already tasked with finding a solution to prevent Social Security's 
approaching trust fund insolvency.

 Bottom line
Neither proposed bill has been signed into law, and at this time, the idea of 
using the CPI-E remains a proposal, not a planned change. The 2027 COLA should 
increase Social Security benefits by an average of $75 per month in 2027, 
meaning nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries should see that boost. 
The increase begins in January 2027 for Social Security beneficiaries, while 
individuals receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI) should see their 
increase begin on December 31, 2026. 
You may access your COLA notice, including your 2027 benefit amount, by logging 
into your my Social Security account and signing up for paperless billing 
beginning in late November. Once you've identified your monthly benefit amount, 
you may want to revisit your retirement plan and budget to make any adjustments needed.
